title: Use a comparison only when the viewer must weigh the same criteria on both sides.
summary: This edge fixture pushes text density with six criteria rows, longer labels, and asymmetrical column copy while staying within the portrait safe area.
footer: Reduced-motion mode swaps directional movement for short opacity reveals.

callout.label: Selection rule
callout.value: If the answer is obvious without the second column, a simple list is usually faster.

criteria.label: Viewer needs only one recommended action
criteria.leftValue: Lead with a headline and three supporting bullets.
criteria.rightValue: Too much structure for a single recommendation.

criteria.label: Viewer must inspect tradeoffs across the exact same decision points
criteria.leftValue: Bullets hide which criterion each option answers.
criteria.rightValue: Aligned rows let the tradeoff stay explicit.

criteria.label: Narration is short and should land in under five seconds
criteria.leftValue: The simpler layout keeps reading friction low.
criteria.rightValue: Only use if comparison is the whole point of the scene.

criteria.label: One side includes caveats, exceptions, or longer explanatory phrasing
criteria.leftValue: Extra nuance can make the list feel uneven and harder to scan.
criteria.rightValue: Row alignment contains longer copy without losing structure.

criteria.label: The director needs a dense edge-case surface for teaching or review content
criteria.leftValue: Possible, but more likely to feel like stacked notes.
criteria.rightValue: This family keeps density organized with rules and restrained accents.

criteria.label: The team expects to reuse the frame across multiple family topics
criteria.leftValue: Easy for one-off explainers and short reminders.
criteria.rightValue: Best when the comparison grammar itself is part of the lesson.
